title: I created a GUI wrapper for Cloudflare WARP for linux
body:
1. Problem

I recently migrated to linux full time because of a corrupted windows installation (I played with magnets around my hard drive), and I use Cloudflare WARP a lot to be able to browse website's blocked by my school's wifi (they blocked github, so don't judge me), and I had a problem with checking the status of the VPN's connection as I would need to open the terminal and keep spamming warp-cli status to see when it connects, and I got sick of that, I needed a GUI similar to the one on windows, the one that lives in the tray and shows a tiny window when clicked, and there IS one on linux, but it's only the Zero Trust version, which is free but needs payment verification which is a hassle because of my age and where I'm from, soooo... I decided to make my own GUI with some improvements over the windows version and the Zero Trust version.

2. Solution

After thinking of how I would make this GUI interact with the WARP service (warp-svc), I realised I could just make the UI a frontend wrapper that interacts with WARP using the warp-cli as a backend, and I was trying to learn PyQt to be able to make clean, linux friendly GUIs, but exams were closing in, so I did something controvertial and used Claude to help with the UI stuff, and yes, I've reviewed the code and I know what I'm doing, it's safe, I've already been beaten up for it enough on reddit, I swear I know what I'm doing 🙏.

This was what I started with, a simple proof of concept:

And this is the lastest version (v1.1) as of the release of this post:

3. Conclusion

The wrapper offers a clean GUI, it's animated in some areas, it has live status updates (So i finally don't have to keep spamming warp-cli status), it allows you to switch modes easily, has a built-in terminal if you still want to run commands, has a restart service button (requires root...), and stays in system tray with a colored icon that shows you the connection status.

title: Rational Irrationality
body:
Prelude:

The Prisoner's Dilemma

Imagine the following scenario: Two suspects are arrested, held in isolation, and offered a deal by police. The prisoners are presented with a dilemma, each prisoner can either cooperate (remain silent) or defect (betray the partner and confess). In the case where both prisoners cooperate, both of them serve a short senstence, however if they both defect, they both serve a medium sentence, and if one defects while the other cooperates, the defector goes free while the cooperator serves the maximum sentence.

For simplification, the short sentence is 1 year, the medium is 5, the maximum is 10.

This scenario is a thought expirement called the "Prisoner's Dilemma", a game described in William Poundstone's 1993 book Prisoner's Dilemma, so let's go through the thought process of prisoner A:
1. If prisoner A assumes B will defect, then A's optimal/safest choice would be to also defect and suffer the 5 year sentence for mutual defection instead of the 10 year sentence.
1. If A assumes B will cooperate, then A's optimal choice now would be to also defect, since going free is better than serving a 1 year sentence.

So regardless of B's strategy, A will always defect, and with parallel reasoning, B will also always defect, that's because defection always results in a better payoff than cooperation, so it is a strictly dominant strategy for both players. Mutual defection is the only strong Nash equilibrium in the game.

In game theory, a Nash equilibrium is a situation where no player could gain more by changing their own strategy (holding all other players' strategies fixed) in a game. A Nash equilibrium is the most commonly used solution concept for non-cooperative games.

If each player has chosen a strategy — an action plan based on what has happened so far in the game — and no one can increase one's own expected payoff by changing one's strategy while the other players keep theirs unchanged, then the current set of strategy choices constitutes a Nash equilibrium.

So after knowing all of this, as a prisoner the rational choice is to always defect, which would almost always lead to either going free, or getting the 5 year sentence.

The Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma

If two players play the prisoner's dilemma more than once in succession, remember their opponent's previous actions, and are allowed to change their strategy accordingly, the game is called the iterated prisoner's dilemma.

In the iterated prisoner's dilemma, the rational strategy isn't immediately obvious, suddenly the strategy of always defecting isn't as obviously rational as before, despite the same rules of the game applying here, a lot has changed when it comes to the optimal thought process to reach maximum benifet.

If the iterated prisoner's dilemma is played a finite number of times and both players know this, then the dominant strategy and Nash equilibrium is to defect in all rounds. The proof is inductive: one might as well defect on the last turn, since the opponent will not have a chance to later retaliate. Therefore, both will defect on the last turn. Thus, the player might as well defect on the second-to-last turn, since the opponent will defect on the last no matter what is done, and so on. The same applies if the game length is unknown but has a known upper limit.

How cooperation emerges and why the Irrational choice suddenly becomes rational?

For cooperation to emerge between rational players, the number of rounds must be unknown or infinite. In that case, "always defect" may no longer be a dominant strategy. Here's where the rational choice might not be so rational any more. As shown by Robert Aumann in a 1959 paper, rational players interacting for an indefinate amount of games eventually start to sustain cooperation, becuase their views have changed, if one game is played the prisoners only look out for their own self-interest, but in an indefinate amount of games cooperative behavior emerges, and that doesn't mean they're now choosing the irrational choice, they just finally saw the benifet in cooperation.

Let's say the prisoners are going to play a hundred successive games, and they know the number of games they're about to play. In this scenario if both players defect every round because of how rational defection seems from their personal stand-point, both players get the medium sentence every time, resulting in a sentence of 500 years, but if both look at the bigger picture, and evaluate the irrational choices over the long run, they'll see that mutual cooperation over the entirety of the 100 games, each player will recieve a sentence of 100 years which is definately better than a 500 year sentence, so suddenly the previously ditched option of cooperating comes back on the table for both player.
Here you might ask, what if the players don't pick the same choice? Well in that case the prisoner is risking losing the other's trust or disappointing them, which might cause them to retaliate by defecting in the next round, and it might even turn into a tit-for-tat situation, or a grimm trigger situation.

Tit-for-tat strategy

It's a strategy where each player mimics the action of the other player in the previous round as gratitude for cooperation or retatliation for defection. In that case both players will keep switching sides, which means that every two rounds both players get 10 years added to their sentence, so agter the full 100 rounds the result is another 500 year sentence for both players.

Grimm trigger strategy

One player might cooperate initially until triggered by a defection from the opponent, which causes the first player to switch approaches and defect every time until the end of the game. The only way to avoid a grim trigger as the opponent is to cooperate until the very last round, which is impossible to do reliably when the number of rounds is unknown.

Comparison between the two strategies

Tit for tat and grim trigger strategies are similar in nature in that both are trigger strategies where a player refuses to defect first if he has the ability to punish the opponent for defecting. The difference, however, is that grim trigger seeks maximal punishment for a single defection while tit for tat is more forgiving, offering one punishment for each defection.

Thoughts

When I first read about this thought expirement I thought it was just kind of fun, but after thinking about it deeper and reading more, it's actually more important than I thought. The game respresents many situations we face every day and the strategies followed in the game could be applied to those situations and to even grander concepts and more important fields. It also taught me that the most rational choice isn't always the most obvious or safest, and sometimes one has to take the risk to get the best outcome. Sometimes you have to think about the long run, not just now, and personally I think that's beautiful.

Ever since I read about this game I've been facinated by its implications. My perspective on life has changed a lot, and I try to apply the lessons I learned from it in any aspect of my life.
